about: The words of the chain silver_road (Data/encounters/chain_silver_road_793.json; Design/content/chains/silver_road.md): the road east to Aldeigjuborg and the silver of the Caliphate. Every title, intention, line and label key of its fourteen cards; an outcome text for every option (keys '...out_<option>', named in each option's note: the engine shows the effects' own facts, the outcome texts are for the integrator); the news items its endings post; and an 'art.<card id>' line for each card's picture. Nobody in these years says 'dirham' or 'Rus': it is the Saracens' silver, the writing silver, the east road, Aldeigja. Nothing here is quoted from any book: all of it is our own wording. Holmfast (cast.holmfast) says the number first and repeats your offer back to you. Vigmund, Botmund and the boy Folkbern are invented. Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: A coin with no face

On the dam a Svea trader is paying for wine. He does not count his silver, he weighs it, on a small scale that folds into a bronze case. Among the cut pieces lies a thin broad coin with writing on both sides and no king's head. The moneyer has come down from the upper town to look at it.
Three casks. I said three and I have counted three. Now the silver. Watch the beam, not my hand.
It weighs a penny and two thirds. The silver is better than mine. There is no head on it, no cross, no name I can read. Who strikes a coin and does not sign it?
The king's law says his penny is taken at its face in every market. This has no face. So it is only silver, and silver I may buy.
You carry a scale. Good. Then we need not talk about whose head is on anything.
You have no scale. Then you take my word for the weight, or his. I would not take either.
Buy the coin for its weight and half again, and give it to the moneyer to study
Sell him a cask of wine on his own scale
Ask him where such silver comes from

The Svea repeats your offer slowly, weighs the coin once more, and takes it. The moneyer carries the thing up the hill in both hands. That night there is a lamp in the mint long after the anvil is quiet.

You watch the beam and not his hand. It comes level, and stays level when he takes his fingers away. He pays in cut silver and one thin coin with writing, and you find you have sold a cask for more than the dam has paid all summer.
The beam comes level, you think. He did not cheat you: you cannot yet read a scale, and he is not a man to point out an error in his own favour. It is still more than the dam pays.

From the east, he says. Past Birka, past the sea, up a river, and then other men bring it up other rivers. He has never seen the men who strike it. Come to Birka in the summer market, he says: wine is dear there, and he will show you a bowlful.
Counted twice

At Birka nobody asks whose head is on your silver. Holmfast's booth has furs to the roof, a scale on a peg, and a bowl of coins cut in halves and quarters like cheese. The man in the next booth offers to lend you his own scale. He steadies the beam with his thumb.
The Frisian from the Rhine. I said to my son a Frisian would come this summer or the next. He said the next. He owes me a marten.
You bought the coin with the writing and gave it away to a man who makes coins. I have counted that twice. It comes out better than it sounds.
Here a coin is silver or it is not. You cut it to make the weight. You nick the edge to see what is under the skin. A king's name does not make lead any lighter.
Eight ounces to the mark. My weights are lead with a bronze coat, and every one has been on Holmfast's scale. He sent two back.
Buy a scale and a bag of weights, and have Holmfast teach you the nick
Trade on the neighbour's scale and watch his thumb
Sit a day by his booth and watch the weighing

Two pans, a beam that folds, a case that shuts with a hook. Holmfast makes you weigh the same quarter-coin nine times, until you get the same answer nine times. Then he shows you the nick: a knife's point on the edge, and bright metal or dull. By evening the next booth has stopped offering to help you.
You watch the thumb. When it comes near the beam you stop talking and look at it, and it goes away again. Holmfast, at his own booth, counts something on his fingers and almost smiles.
You watched the thumb. You did not watch the weights, which were his too. Holmfast says nothing. He has seen it done to better men, and he lets a lesson finish before he speaks of it.

You sit on a bale all day. He weighs, cuts, nicks, and marks each sale on a stick in short straight strokes that you begin to tell apart. Nobody is cheated at his booth. Two men are cheated at the next one.
What the east wants

Holmfast is baling skins for the winter. He goes east when the ice lets go of the bay and comes home with the silver before the night frosts. He has been thinking about what a man from the Rhine could put in his ship.

Five days east over the sea. A short river, a wide lake, another river. A place called Aldeigja. There the skins come out of the woods and the silver comes up from the south. I buy one with the other.

They want three things I cannot make. Blades from your smiths, without hilts: they hilt them their own way. Glass beads, green ones first. Wine. For a good blade they give what I give for forty marten.
Your king forbids mail coats to leave his land. A Frisian told me. He has said nothing yet about a bare blade. Kings think of things late.
Your king now forbids arms to leave his land at all, and takes the ship of the man who tries. A Frisian told me. A forbidden blade weighs the same. It is your neck; I only say what it would fetch.
Come next summer when the birch is in leaf. We sail east four ships together. Bring what you bring. I will count it.
Promise him four blades from the Rhine smiths
Promise beads and wine, which no toll man will take your boat for
Promise nothing; say you will come and see
Four blades, he says back to you. Four. He lays a timber of squirrel on your arm as earnest and does not ask how you will get them past your own toll man. That is your side of the sea.

Beads and wine, he says back to you. He thinks about it for the time it takes to tie a bale. Then he lays a timber of squirrel on your arm as earnest. A man who keeps his boat, he says, comes back a second year.
You will come and see, he says back to you. He nods and goes on baling. He has counted nothing, so there is nothing for him to count twice.
Low in the water

A Gotland boat lies low in the water with her steering oar gone and a lee shore half a mile under her. Her men bail and do not wave. There is a chest amidships with a hide lashed over it, and nobody aboard her looks at it.
We have lost an oar. I would not call it more than that. If you have one to spare, I will remember where I got it.
That is ballast. We find it steadies her.
Lay alongside, give her your spare oar and tow her off the shore
Name a price for the tow before you throw the line
Stand by to windward until the wind eases, and do no more

The line holds. You drag her head round a boat's length at a time until she has water under her and your oar on her quarter. Her skipper is Botmund, of Paviken on Gotland. He hands over a fistful of thin silver with writing on it and does not count it, which from a Gotlander is a speech.

The line parts and takes the skin off a man's hand on your own boat. An hour later the wind backs and she claws off by herself, with your oar. Her skipper, Botmund of Paviken, calls over the water that he saw who tried.

He looks at the shore, then at you, and names a weight of silver before you can. He pays it out of the chest that is ballast, in thin coins with writing. He does not give his name, and he does not ask yours. He will know the boat.

You lie to windward of her through the afternoon, which costs you the afternoon. Towards evening the wind eases and she rows off the shore with a plank lashed for a steering oar. A man in her stern lifts one hand, once.
In company
Four ships lie loaded off Birka's jetties, Holmfast's among them. They sail east together or not at all. He looks at your boat, which is the smallest thing in the bay, and then at what is in it.
The birch is in leaf and here is the Frisian. My son said you would not come. He owes me a second marten.
Four blades, you said. I have told a man in the east four. I do not like to tell a man a number twice.
Beads and wine, you said. I have told nobody, because beads break and wine is drunk on the way. Show me.
After the short river there is a lake with no far shore. It is shallow and it stands up in a north wind. We cross it in the night calm or we wait. Men who do not wait are found in the reeds.
On the south shore of the gulf there are men in small boats who count ships. Four they let pass. One they follow. Keep where I can see your sail.
Show him the blades under the ballast
Show him beads and wine
Come as you are and offer to keep his tally

He draws one a hand's breadth out of its greased wool, flexes it against the thwart and lets it spring back. Four, he says. Then he tells his steersman to give you the place astern of him, which is the safe one.

He holds a string of green beads up to the light and counts a cask by knocking on it. It will do, he says. The men of the woods take beads before silver; he does not know why and has stopped asking. You sail third of five.

He looks into your empty boat for some time. Then he hands you his tally stick and a knife. If you cut one notch wrong, he says, he will know by Aldeigja. You sail last of five, and learn to count in his tongue on the way.
The landing at Aldeigja

The river is brown and fast, and the sea ships go no further: above the town it breaks over rock. Log houses, a smithy, skins stacked like firewood, wax in cakes. Men from the woods stand apart with their bundles and speak a tongue nobody on your boat knows. In the biggest house a man named Vigmund weighs out thin silver with writing on it.
This is a Frisian from the Rhine. I have weighed with him two summers. His weights agree with mine.
From the Rhine. That is further than I can think. Sit. Nobody here is anybody's king; you deal with me because my house has the most roof.

It comes up from the south, from men who come from other men. Some pieces have marks scratched on them by every hand they passed. I have one with four kinds of scratching. I cannot read any of it. It weighs true.
Holmfast says you have blades. Lay them on the bench. I pay for those before I pay for anything.
No blades. A pity. The men down the rivers ask me for blades first and everything else second. Show me what you have.
Sell him the four blades
Sell him ten strings of beads
Sell him three casks of Rhine wine
Sell nothing; keep Holmfast's tally through the selling and take a hand's share

He bends each blade over his knee and listens to it. Then he weighs out silver until your scale pan will hold no more, and starts again, and throws a timber of marten on top as if it were a rag. You have never been paid like this for anything. He asks the smith's name. You find you would rather not say.

He does not want the beads himself. He walks them over to the men from the woods, who do, and comes back with two bundles of beaver he did not have before. Then he pays you in silver for the trouble of having stood between.

He has the first cask opened on the landing and drinks standing. Wine has come this far before, he says, but sour. He pays in thin silver and a cake of wax, and has the other two casks carried into his own house and not the storehouse.

You cut Holmfast's notches for three days while skins go one way and silver the other. Not one notch is wrong. He pays you a hand's share and two timbers of squirrel, and you have seen every price on the river without paying for one of them.
What the silver buys

Vigmund walks you behind his house to show you what goes south. A pen of split logs, roofed at one end. Some twenty people sit in it, roped by the neck in fours: Slavs from up the river, two women who speak something like Danish, and a boy with a tally stick who looks up when he hears your crew talk.
You think the silver comes for skins. Some does. A boatload of skins brings a bag. A boatload of these brings a chest. The men in the south have no end of silver and never enough hands.
Are you from the Rhine? I am Folkbern. I was ship's boy on a boat out of Wijnaldum. They took us off the Danish coast two summers back. The others were sold south. I can count, so he kept me.
That one talks like you. He keeps my tally and has not cut a wrong notch yet. I would rather keep him. A mark and two ounces, weighed, and I will have to learn to count again.
Or this. Your coast is full of people and your boat has room. Bring me six next summer, sound and young. I pay what Holmfast has never seen, and I pay it to you and not to him.
Weigh out a mark and two ounces and take the boy home
Give him your hand on six, sound and young, by next summer
Say your boat carries things that do not need feeding

You weigh it out on your own scale and he checks it on his. He cuts the rope himself, with some regret, and takes back the tally stick. The boy walks to your boat without looking round at the pen. He does not speak until the town is out of sight, and then he asks what day of the Church's year it is.

He takes your hand and holds it a moment longer than a bargain needs, looking at you to see what kind of man it is. Then he weighs out an earnest in cut silver. Behind him the boy with the tally stick has gone back to looking at the ground.
He shrugs. Skins do not eat, he agrees, and they do not fetch much either. He walks you back round to the front of the house. Nobody in the pen had looked up for long.
Under the floor
Paviken smells of tar and hot iron. A shipwright named Botmund is laying a new floor of planks in his storehouse, over ground that was dug not long ago. He sees you look, and goes on laying planks.
The Frisian with the spare oar. I said I would remember where I got it. It is on that wall. Sit down.
A Frisian. They say you have been to Aldeigja in the Svea's wake. A long way to follow another man's stern.
A floor keeps the damp out. Every house on this island has a good floor. We do not talk about floors.

The Svea shows a man the way east and takes a skin in ten from him for ever after. I take a fee once and forget your name. I know the short river and the lake as well as he does. He will not thank you.
Take his pilotage on the strength of the oar you lent him
Pay him his fee, once, and go east next summer without the Svea
Say you went east with Holmfast and will go east with Holmfast

He nods and lays another plank. Next summer, he says, when the ice is out of the gulf: come here first and not to Birka, and tell nobody at Birka. He does not shake hands on it. On Gotland a thing said once has been said.

He looks at you over the plank for a while. That is an answer too, he says, and not a bad one to hear from a man you might sail with. Then, because you asked for nothing, he tells you what the island is short of this year. It is cloth.
Twenty and thirty-four

You tip a bag of the east's silver onto the moneyer's bench in the upper town: whole coins, halves, quarters, all writing and no face. He weighs twenty of the whole ones against the king's pennies, and then does it again.
You brought me one of these before. I have it still. I have looked at it more nights than I would tell my wife. Now you bring a bag.
Twenty of these weigh what thirty-four of the king's pennies weigh. And the silver is better than mine. I do not like that. I should like to know who does it, and how.

A pilgrim back from Rome showed me the like. It is the Saracens' writing. They put no face on their coin; their law forbids images, he said. What the words say he did not know. Nothing about our Lord, I should think.
By the king's law I take only his penny at its face. This has no face, so it is bullion, and bullion I may buy for the pot. What comes out will have his name on it and be none the worse.
Is there more where this was? I do not mean a bag.
Sell him the bag for the pot, less his cut, and promise him more
Keep it whole: north of the Eider it buys more than his pennies do
Give him one whole coin to keep and ask only what he makes of it

It goes into the pot that afternoon and comes out as the king's pennies, more of them than you had reckoned, because the silver was better than he is used to. He takes his cut and for once does not round it up. Bring more, he says. He will speak to the count's steward about a man who brings silver into the realm and not out of it.

You sweep it back into the bag. He watches every piece go. North of the Eider nobody melts good silver to put a name on it, and a man who can reckon the king's penny, the cut piece and the writing coin against each other is cheated by none of the three.

He turns it over and over. Every one the same breadth, he says, and the letters as fine on the last as on the first. Whoever does this has more silver than the king and more moneyers than Francia. He puts it away where the first one is, and says your word on foreign silver is good at this bench.
Three kinds of silver
The purse is open on a thwart: the king's pennies, cut silver from Birka, and the thin coins with writing. Two of your men were asked what the boat is worth, and they have two answers.
That is a penny. It has the king's name on it and the count's man must take it. The rest is scrap. I would not give you a herring for what a heathen scratched on a bit of plate.
I have tried your penny with a knife. It is a good penny. It is mostly silver. The writing ones are all silver. I know which I would rather be owed.
And who wrote on it? Nobody you can find and bring before a court. A coin should have someone to hang.
Kings die. All of them, I hear. Silver I have never seen do it.
Put it all on the scale: silver is what it weighs
Change it all at the next mint and know what you have
Let them argue; it passes the watch
You weigh the whole purse on the thwart, piece by piece, with the boat lifting under the scale. It comes to more than either of them said. The Dane looks pleased and the Frisian looks at the horizon.
At the next mint, you say, it all goes in the pot and comes out with a name on it. The Frisian is content. The Dane says a moneyer's cut is the only toll a man pays twice and thanks the taker for.
They are still at it when the watch changes. By then it is about whether a king or a scale has ever been wrong, and the whole boat has taken a side. Nobody has been this cheerful since the last port.
One purse
Holmfast has set out two stools and a scale at his booth, and ale, which he does not often buy. A silver arm ring lies on the bench between the stools.
Three summers. You came when you said you would come. Your weights agree with mine. I have counted you twice.
The blades cut. Vigmund asked me the smith's name. I did not have it to give, which saved me refusing.

You paid a mark and two ounces for a boy and then gave him away. I have counted that three times and it is a loss each time. Still. A man who pays for a thing and does what he said with it: I can sail with that.
A Gotlander offered you my road for a fee. I hear things. You said no. He told it himself, as a thing against you.

So. One purse for the east goods. I sail east, you sail west. Skins and wax to the Rhine, wine and beads and what else you dare to me. We halve it here each summer when the birch is in leaf. Say it back to me.
Swear it his way, with your hand on the ring
Swear it your own way and let him swear his
No oath: a price each summer, and a man of yours kept at his booth

You lay your hand on the ring and say it back to him, word for word, and he says it to you. Then he weighs out your half of this summer's purse, which he had ready. It is a great deal. Your crew, who are baptised men, say nothing about the ring until Birka is astern, and then a good deal.

You swear by your own God with your hand on your own breast, and he swears on his ring. He turns that over: two oaths, two witnesses in two heavens. Harder to break than one, he decides. Then he weighs out your half of this summer's purse, which he had ready.

No oath, he says back to you. A price each summer and your man on a stool at his booth, watching. He thinks it a thin way to do a fat trade, and says so, once. Then he weighs out this summer's price to the grain.
Six, sound and young
Vigmund has the six brought up from your boat and looks at their teeth and their hands. The Frisian boy stands behind him with the tally stick, a year taller, and cuts six notches without looking up.
Six. You gave your hand on six and here are six. I had a marten on it with Holmfast that you would not.
I said I would pay what the Svea has never seen. Bring your scale. We will be some time.
Six. Four men and two women. One of the women speaks my tongue. I have cut it as six.
And there is a ship on my bank that a man left me for a debt. She is too deep for the river and I do not go to sea. You will need a bigger hull for this trade. Take her as part.
Take the silver and the ship
Take less silver, the ship, and the Frisian boy
Turn back at his door: say the bargain is off

It takes until dark to weigh. The six are walked round behind the house. You do not go with them. You sail in a ship twice the length of the boat you came in, with more silver than the count's steward sees in a year, and the story is at Dorestad before you are. A priest there will know your name now, and not for alms.

Vigmund laughs: a dealer in people with a soft place, he says, and it is the first time anyone has called you that to your face. He cuts the boy's rope. The boy comes aboard the new ship and sits as far forward as he can get. He is going home. He also cut the six notches, and you both know it.

He does not shout. He tells you what a hand is worth on this river once it has been given and taken back, and it is not much. The six are still in your boat, and they are still yours to answer for. Holmfast's road is open to you yet. This man's door is not.
A mark and two ounces

A man on the landing knows the boy's face before the boy knows his. It is his mother's brother. By evening there are kin enough to fill the boat, and cloth and a little silver laid out on a cloak in front of you.
I come up to the dams every year with the terp's cloth. Two years I have asked every boat from the north for a boy named Folkbern. I had stopped asking this summer. God forgive me that.
His mother saw the sail from the terp and said it was nobody's she knew. Then she saw who was in the bow. You will have to forgive the noise. Nobody here has had anyone back before.
We know what a boy costs in those places. We are not rich. This is the terp's cloth for the year and what silver six houses have. Take it. We will not have it said that a stranger paid for our blood.

I can count their way. I can talk to the Svear, and some to the men who bring the skins. Nobody on this coast can. Send me back when the ice goes, as your man, with a house to answer to. I would sooner go back there free than stay here owing.
Take what his kin lay down
Take back the mark and two ounces, and not a penny over
Take nothing; ask only that the boy sail with you when he is ready

You take it, and it is fair, and they are easier for having paid. The cloth is good. In the spring the boy goes east in a Svea ship with your mark on a stick, to sit at Aldeigja and count for your house. He is nobody's thrall and nobody's son there. He is your man.

You weigh a mark and two ounces out of their silver on your own scale, in front of all of them, and push the rest back across the cloak. The uncle says that is how a debt between honest men ends. In the spring the boy goes east with your mark on a stick, to count for your house at Aldeigja.

You push the cloak back. There is a long quiet. Then his mother takes your hand and puts the boy's in it, before witnesses, and that is a fostering on this coast, and he is of your house. In the morning the cloth is in your boat all the same, and the silver under it, and nobody will say who put it there. He sails with you. In the spring he goes east.
Ground on the Volkhov

Botmund has brought you up the short river and over the lake in a night calm, and you lie at Aldeigja a week before any ship from Birka. Vigmund comes down to the landing himself. He counts your crew, then looks behind you for a sail that is not there.
You come without the Svea. Then his tenth stays in your purse or in mine. Let us weigh which.

There is ground between my house and the smithy. Put a house on it and a man in the house, and I deal with you before any ship from Birka is in the river. Nobody from the Rhine has ever wintered here. I should like to see if it can be done.
I said I would forget your name. I say one thing more and then I do. Build above the line the spring ice leaves on the bank. The river does not care whose house it is.
They tell me you have a man at home who melts my silver and puts your king's name on it. Good. Silver that turns into something else comes back wanting more silver.
Holmfast will know by the next moon. He counts everything twice. He will count this more often.
Take the ground, and carry the silver straight to the pot on the Rhine
Take the ground, and keep the silver working in the north
Take the ground, and send Holmfast a third with your word on it

Four posts go into the bank above the ice line, and a man of yours stays to roof them. You carry home a chest, not a bag, and the moneyer at Dorestad works three nights on it. The pennies that leave his bench that week have the king's name on them and the east's silver in them, and nobody who spends one will ever know. Botmund has told you the lake and the river once, and you have them. At Birka a Svea trader has stopped saying your name.

Four posts go into the bank above the ice line, and a man of yours stays to roof them. The silver you keep whole and working, at Paviken, at Birka's far jetty, at Sliesthorp: it buys more there than any pot would give you for it. At Holmfast's booth they have stopped saying your name.

Four posts go into the bank above the ice line. A third of the purse goes to Birka by Botmund's hand with a stick cut in your own notches: the tenth was his, here is more than the tenth, the road is wide enough. Word comes back before the ice. It is one notch, which in his tally means counted, and nothing else. It is not friendship. It is not a feud either.
The moneyer in the upper town has been buying foreign silver for the pot: thin broad coins with writing and no king's head. He says it is better than his own and will not say who brought it.
A house of Dorestad has sworn one purse with a Svea of Birka. Marten and wax from beyond the eastern sea will come up the Rhine each summer, and the wine goes back the same way.

A boat of Dorestad went east with people under her deck and came home a ship. The priests of the upper town have the name of her master. So has the count's steward, who has read the king's law on selling Christians aloud at the toll.
A ship's boy of Westergo, taken by sea-robbers two summers ago and sold beyond the eastern sea, has come home alive. A merchant of Dorestad weighed out his price to a heathen and brought him back.
A house of Dorestad has put up a storehouse on a river beyond the eastern sea, where no Frisian has wintered before. The mint in the upper town has not been so busy since the king made the new penny.
A Frisian has taken ground at Aldeigja and brought his own ship in a week before the Birka fleet, with a Gotlander at the steering oar. Nobody at Birka is pleased, and one man there least of all.

Dorestad, a timber dam at midday in summer: a spare, pale-eyed Svea in a fur-trimmed cap holds a small folding scale over a wine cask; a stooped moneyer in a leather apron bends close to one thin broad coin in the pan. Boats and the river behind.

Birka, a booth on the jetty in clear northern morning light: furs stacked to the roof, a bowl of coins cut in halves and quarters, the Svea showing a knife-nick on a coin's edge; in the next booth a man with his thumb on a scale beam.

Birka at dusk, late summer: the Svea kneeling on a bale of skins to rope it, talking over his shoulder; behind him his ship drawn up on the shore for the winter, and a bare sword blade drawn with a finger in the dust of the floor.

The open Baltic, grey afternoon, a hard wind: a Gotland boat low in the water with no steering oar, men bailing, a hide-covered chest amidships; a low dark shore with breakers close under her; your small boat coming down from windward.

Birka's bay early on a bright day in first summer, the birches in new leaf: four loaded ships at anchor and one very small Frisian boat alongside the nearest; the Svea leaning over his gunwale to look down into her.

Aldeigja on the brown Volkhov under a low white sky: log houses on a bank, skins stacked like firewood, wax cakes, trappers in hide coats standing apart; in a doorway a heavy man weighs thin silver on a scale; white water on rock upstream.

Behind a log house in flat evening light: a pen of split logs, people sitting roped by the neck in fours, faces turned down; one boy of thirteen with cropped hair and a tally stick looking straight out at the viewer; the dealer's back, pointing.

Paviken on Gotland, inside a storehouse with the door open to a bright beach and a half-built hull: a shipwright on his knees laying floor planks over freshly dug earth, not looking up; an oar hung on the wall behind him.

The mint in Dorestad's upper town by lamplight: a heap of whole and cut coins covered in writing on a bench, the moneyer holding a balance with twenty of them against a pile of pennies; a priest peering at one coin held to the lamp; anvil and dies behind.

Aboard the boat at sea in a fair wind, late afternoon: an open purse on a thwart with three little heaps of silver; a Dane testing a penny's edge with his knife, a Frisian hand jabbing a finger at him, the rest of the crew grinning.

Birka, the booth at midsummer evening, long light: two stools, a jug of ale, a scale, and a plain silver arm ring on the bench between the Svea and the Frisian merchant, who faces him; a divided heap of silver ready at the Svea's elbow.

Aldeigja's landing in hard noon light: six roped people standing in a row on the bank, the dealer looking at one man's teeth; behind him the Frisian boy cutting notches in a stick, eyes down; a long sea-going ship lying empty against the bank.

A Frisian landing under a wide evening sky, a terp on the skyline: a boy held hard by a woman and a big farmer, kin crowding round; in front of the merchant a cloak spread on the ground with folded cloth and a small heap of silver on it.

The bank of the Volkhov early on a still morning, mist on the water: four new posts of a house standing in bare ground between a big log house and a smithy; the dealer pacing out the plot, a Gotlander pointing at the ice line on the bank, one small Frisian boat alone at the landing.
